lessons.title: The Media Industry: Sectors & Products
lessons.description: Explore the major sectors of the media industry and the diverse products each one creates.
lessons.content_html:
What Is the Media Industry?

The media industry is one of the largest and fastest-changing economic sectors in the UK. It encompasses every organisation involved in creating, producing and distributing content to audiences — from Hollywood blockbusters and chart-topping podcasts to smartphone apps and billboard advertisements. Understanding how the industry is organised into distinct sectors is the foundation of your study of Creative iMedia.

The Sectors of the Media Industry

The media industry is divided into several major sectors. The television and film sector produces moving-image content for broadcast TV channels, streaming platforms such as Netflix and BBC iPlayer, and cinema release. The publishing sector covers books, magazines, newspapers and digital publications. Advertising and marketing creates promotional content across every medium — from TV commercials and social media campaigns to physical posters. The games sector develops interactive software for consoles, PCs and mobile devices. Finally, the web and app sector designs and builds websites, mobile applications and digital services. Each sector has its own production methods, job roles and target audiences.

Key Fact

The five main sectors of the media industry are: television and film; publishing; advertising and marketing; games; and web and app. Each sector produces different types of media product and employs specialists with different skill sets.

Types of Media Product

Within and across sectors, media professionals create a wide range of media products. Moving image products include films, TV programmes, animations and music videos. Audio products include radio broadcasts, podcasts, sound effects and music tracks. Publishing and print products encompass newspapers, magazines, leaflets, posters and books. Interactive products — such as websites, apps and e-learning modules — invite the audience to engage rather than simply watch or listen. Games are a product category in their own right, ranging from console titles to casual mobile games. Audio-visual products combine sound and moving image, such as TV adverts, corporate videos and online tutorials.

How Media Products Combine Different Media

In practice, the boundaries between product types are blurring. A modern marketing campaign might consist of a TV advert (audio-visual), a dedicated website (interactive), social media graphics (publishing/print), and a short podcast series (audio) — all promoting the same brand. A video game may include animated cut-scenes (moving image) alongside its interactive gameplay. The ability to plan, create and combine multiple media types is one of the most valuable skills in the contemporary media industry.

Television and film focuses on producing long-form or short-form moving-image content that is broadcast or distributed to passive audiences — viewers who watch rather than interact. Production is typically expensive, team-based and follows a strict pre-production, production and post-production workflow. The web and app sector, by contrast, creates digital products that users actively navigate and control. Timescales can be shorter, iterative development is common, and the product is often updated continuously after launch. Despite these differences, both sectors rely on creative planning, technical skill and an understanding of the target audience.

The Scale and Reach of the Media Industry

The UK media industry contributes billions of pounds to the economy each year and employs hundreds of thousands of people. The rise of streaming, social media and on-demand content has disrupted traditional business models — print newspaper circulation has fallen sharply while podcast audiences have grown exponentially. Understanding these changes helps media creators plan products that can compete in a crowded market and reach audiences on the platforms they actually use.

Key Fact

The six main types of media product are: moving image, audio, publishing and print, interactive, games, and audio-visual. Many modern media campaigns deliberately combine several of these types to reach audiences across multiple platforms.

Students often confuse sectors with product types. A sector is an area of the industry (e.g. advertising and marketing); a media product type is the format of the content (e.g. audio-visual). An advertising agency (sector) might produce a TV commercial (audio-visual product type) or a website (interactive product type). In exam answers, be precise: identify both the sector the organisation belongs to and the type of product it creates — they are not interchangeable terms.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to identify a media sector or product type, use the correct terminology and back it up with a real or realistic example. Examiners reward specific, applied knowledge — writing "the games sector produces interactive software such as console games and mobile apps" scores more than simply writing "games". If the question asks you to explain how media products combine types, name both product types involved and describe exactly how they work together in a single product or campaign.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The media industry contains five main sectors — television and film, publishing, advertising and marketing, games, and web and app — each with distinct production methods and audiences.
  • Media products are categorised by type: moving image, audio, publishing and print, interactive, games, and audio-visual; many real-world products deliberately combine several types.
  • Sectors and product types are different things — a sector describes where an organisation sits in the industry, while a product type describes the format of the content it creates.

practice_questions.text:
A media company is planning to launch a campaign for a new sports drink targeting young adults aged 16 to 24. The campaign will include products across three different media types.

Discuss the factors the company should consider when deciding which media types and sectors to use for this campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion addressing at least two relevant factors from different angles, applied to the scenario. For example: the need to reach young adults on the platforms they use most (interactive/social media and audio-visual/short-form video) versus the cost and skill requirements of producing high-quality content across multiple media types; or the benefit of combining product types (e.g. audio-visual TV advert + interactive social media campaign + audio podcast sponsorship) to maximise reach, weighed against the risk of spreading the budget too thinly. Both factors developed with reasoning and scenario reference.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two relevant factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the target audience or campaign context.
Developing (2 marks): One factor identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague point about the campaign with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
The media industry has changed significantly over the last two decades, with streaming platforms replacing traditional broadcast TV for many audiences and digital products overtaking print.

Evaluate the extent to which media creators must understand how different sectors and product types work together in order to succeed in today's media industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues understanding cross-sector, multi-product working is essential because modern audiences consume fragmented content across platforms (streaming, social media, apps, podcasts) so single-sector expertise is insufficient; then challenges this with the counter-argument that deep specialisation within one sector remains valuable — a film editor does not need to build apps — and that large productions rely on specialists, not generalists. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about the relative importance of cross-sector knowledge versus deep specialism, going beyond listing points.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two relevant points on each side, with some application to the changing media landscape and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points identified but largely one-sided or without a judgement. Some reference to sectors or product types.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points about the media industry. [8 marks]

lessons.title: Job Roles & the Production Workflow
lessons.description: Discover who does what in media production and how projects move from idea to finished product.
lessons.content_html:
Who Makes Media?

Creating a media product — whether a film, a website or a video game — is rarely the work of one person. It requires a team of specialists, each responsible for a different aspect of the project. Understanding the key job roles in media production, and the order in which their work happens, is essential both for the exam and for any practical media work you carry out.

Creative and Management Roles

At the top of a production, the producer manages the budget, schedule and overall delivery of a project. They are responsible for making sure the product is finished on time, within budget and to the client's specification. The director makes the creative decisions: visual style, tone, performances and storytelling choices in film and TV productions. In advertising and corporate media, an art director or creative director plays an equivalent role. The graphic designer creates visual assets — logos, layouts, typography and imagery — for print, digital and moving-image products. An animator brings static images or 3D models to life using specialist software such as Adobe After Effects or Autodesk Maya.

Key Fact

Key media job roles include: producer (budget and schedule), director (creative decisions), editor (post-production assembly), graphic designer (visual assets), animator (motion and animation), photographer (stills), web developer (websites and apps), games designer (game rules and experience), and copywriter (written content). Each role has a distinct function in the production process.

Technical and Specialist Roles

The editor assembles raw footage, audio and graphics into the finished product — in film and video they work in editing software such as Adobe Premiere Pro or Final Cut Pro; in publishing they use InDesign to lay out pages. A photographer captures still images for use across print, digital and advertising products. A web developer writes the code that brings a website or app to life, using languages such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A games designer defines the rules, levels, mechanics and player experience of a video game; they work with artists and programmers to translate their vision into a playable product. A copywriter produces all the written text in a media product — advertising straplines, website copy, script dialogue or magazine articles.

This is one of the most commonly confused pairs in the exam. The producer oversees the logistical and financial side of a production: they set the budget, manage the schedule, hire the crew and ensure the project is delivered to the client. The director is responsible for the creative vision: how the product looks, sounds and feels. On a small production, one person might do both jobs, but they remain conceptually distinct. A useful memory hook is: the producer handles the money and the meetings; the director handles the camera and the performances.

The Three Phases of the Production Workflow

All media production — regardless of sector — follows a three-phase production workflow: pre-production, production and post-production. This framework helps teams plan their work, manage resources and deliver a finished product that meets the client's requirements.

Pre-Production, Production and Post-Production

Pre-production covers everything that happens before any content is actually created: writing the script or brief, storyboarding, casting, scouting locations, creating mood boards, planning schedules and budgets, and sourcing assets such as images or music. Production is the active creation phase — filming takes place, photographs are shot, web pages are coded, or game levels are built. Post-production begins once raw content has been gathered: footage is edited, audio is mixed, colour grading is applied, graphics are added, and the product is reviewed and refined before final delivery.

Key Fact

Pre-production (planning): scripts, storyboards, mood boards, schedules, budgets, location scouting. Production (creating): filming, photographing, coding, building. Post-production (finishing): editing, audio mixing, colour grading, graphic overlays, review and final delivery.

Students often write that post-production only means "editing the video". In reality, post-production encompasses a wide range of processes: audio mixing and sound design, music licensing and composition, visual effects (VFX) and colour grading, the creation and integration of motion graphics or animated titles, quality assurance review, and final export or delivery to the client or distributor. In an exam, naming several distinct post-production tasks — not just "editing" — will score significantly higher on explain and describe questions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing a job role, always state clearly what that person does, not just their job title. Examiners want to see understanding: writing "the editor assembles footage, applies colour grading and adds music to create the final cut" scores more than "the editor edits the video". For questions about the production workflow, name the phase and then give at least two specific tasks from that phase — this is especially important for "describe" and "explain" questions worth 3 or more marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Key media job roles include producer (budget and schedule), director (creative decisions), editor (assembly and finishing), graphic designer (visual assets), animator, photographer, web developer, games designer and copywriter — each with a distinct function.
  • All media production follows three phases: pre-production (planning and preparation), production (active creation) and post-production (editing, mixing, review and delivery).
  • The producer manages logistics and budget while the director makes creative decisions — these are separate roles even when one person carries out both.

practice_questions.text:
A small media company has been asked to produce a 3-minute promotional video for a local charity. The team consists of a producer, a director, a videographer and an editor.

Discuss how each job role contributes to the successful completion of this project across the three phases of production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion that links specific job roles to specific tasks within at least two of the three phases, applied to the charity video scenario. For example: the producer sets the schedule and manages the charity client relationship throughout all phases; the director shapes the visual approach in pre-production (concept, storyboard) and directs filming during production; the editor assembles and grades the footage in post-production. Contrast or complexity should be present, e.g. noting that on a small team these roles may overlap, creating scheduling tension.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two roles described with tasks across phases, with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One role or one phase described with limited detail.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague statement about the team with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student argues that pre-production is the most important phase of the production workflow because it determines the success of everything that follows.

A substantiated judgement is reached about the relationship between planning and quality, going beyond a simple list.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two well-developed points on each side with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on the value of pre-production with limited counter-argument.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic statement about planning with no development or evaluation. [8 marks]

lessons.title: Client Requirements & the Target Audience
lessons.description: Learn how to interpret a client brief and use audience profiling to shape every design decision.
lessons.content_html:
Starting with the Client

Every professional media product begins with a client brief. This is the starting point for any production: a written or verbal document in which the client explains what they need, why they need it, who it is for and what constraints apply. Reading and interpreting a client brief accurately is one of the most practical skills examined in the Cambridge National, because all your practical project work in the course begins with a brief provided by the exam board acting as a simulated client.

What a Client Brief Contains

A well-written brief sets out the purpose of the product (to inform, persuade, entertain or promote), the client requirements in terms of content and format, the target audience the product must reach, the delivery deadline and any budget limits. It may also specify technical requirements — file formats, dimensions, platform — and brand guidelines such as colours, fonts and logo usage. When reading a brief, media creators must identify what is fixed (non-negotiable requirements such as the logo or deadline) and what is open to creative interpretation (tone, layout, imagery). Failing to meet a fixed requirement is a professional failure, regardless of how good the creative work is.

Key Fact

A client brief typically specifies: purpose (inform, persuade, entertain, promote); target audience; content requirements; format and technical specifications; budget; and deadline. All creative decisions must be traceable back to these requirements — if a decision cannot be justified by the brief, it is a risk.

Defining the Target Audience

A target audience is the specific group of people a media product is created for. Defining the target audience precisely is essential because every subsequent design decision — from colour palette to reading level, from platform choice to music genre — should be shaped by who will consume the product. A product that tries to appeal to everyone usually appeals to no one.

Demographics: Profiling the Audience

Media professionals use demographics to describe and profile their audience. Key demographic variables include: age (a children's app and a pension provider's website require very different design approaches); gender (though design should avoid harmful stereotyping, gender can influence platform, tone and content choices); income (a luxury brand communicates differently to a budget supermarket); location (local vs national vs global reach affects language, cultural references and distribution platform); and interests and hobbies (knowing an audience is passionate about sport vs music vs gaming shapes every creative decision). Together these variables allow a media creator to build a detailed picture of their audience — sometimes captured in a written audience profile or persona.

Once a creator has built an audience profile, each creative choice can be tested against it. A website targeting 12-to-15-year-olds might use bold, high-contrast colours, short paragraphs, large touch-friendly buttons and informal language — all justified by the age demographic. A financial services website for adults aged 35-55 with high incomes would use a restrained colour palette, professional typography, longer text blocks and formal language. Platform choice is also demographic: a product for teenagers is more likely to be encountered on TikTok or Instagram than on a printed leaflet. Audience profiling turns abstract demographic data into concrete, defensible design decisions.

Audience Segmentation

Large audiences can be divided into sub-groups through a process called audience segmentation. Rather than treating all viewers or users identically, segmentation allows a media creator — or a client — to tailor different versions of a product (or different campaign messages) to different groups. For example, a streaming service might segment its audience by age and recommend different genres to different groups, or a games company might create a family-friendly version and an adult-rated version of the same franchise. Understanding segmentation helps you explain why a single brand might produce several visually and tonally distinct media products aimed at different sub-audiences.

Key Fact

The five key demographic variables used to profile a target audience are: age, gender, income, location and interests. These directly influence design decisions including colour palette, typography, language register, platform choice and content format.

A very common exam mistake is to identify the target audience correctly but then stop there. Simply writing "the target audience is teenagers" gains very few marks. Examiners want to see the link between the audience profile and specific design choices: "because the target audience is teenagers aged 13-16, the website uses bold colours, informal language and a mobile-first layout, as this age group primarily accesses content on smartphones". Every audience statement should be followed immediately by a design implication. This cause-and-effect chain is what separates Mastering-level answers from Developing-level ones.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For any question about client requirements or target audiences, always write in cause-and-effect chains. Do not just identify — connect. A strong answer sounds like: "Because the client brief specifies a target audience of parents with young children (aged 25-40), the designer used pastel colours and rounded fonts to feel approachable and friendly, rather than the bold, high-contrast palette that would be used for a teenage gaming audience." In your practical work, every creative decision in your evidence should reference either the client brief or the audience profile as its justification.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A client brief sets out the purpose, audience, content requirements, format, budget and deadline for a media product; all creative decisions must be traceable back to it.
  • Target audiences are defined using demographic variables — age, gender, income, location and interests — which directly shape every design decision from colour palette to platform choice.
  • Audience statements must be followed by design implications; simply naming a target audience without linking it to specific creative choices scores minimal marks in the exam.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'audience segmentation'. Give one example of how a media company might use it.

lessons.title: Media Codes, Conventions & Genre
lessons.description: Understand how media codes, genre conventions and tone communicate meaning to an audience.
lessons.content_html:
How Media Communicates Meaning

Every element of a media product — the choice of colour, the angle of a camera shot, the font on a poster — communicates something to the audience. Media professionals call these elements media codes. Understanding codes is central to creating media that works: a product that uses codes effectively guides its audience to the right interpretation; one that uses them badly creates confusion or sends the wrong message. Your task as a media creator is to make deliberate, justifiable coding choices.

Visual and Technical Codes

Camera codes in moving image include shot size (a close-up creates intimacy; a wide shot establishes setting), camera angle (a low angle makes a subject look powerful; a high angle can make them appear vulnerable) and camera movement (a tracking shot follows action, creating energy). Layout codes in graphic design and publishing govern how elements are arranged on a page or screen: the rule of thirds, visual hierarchy, the use of white space and the placement of the most important information where the eye travels first. Colour codes exploit the associations audiences bring to colours: red can signify danger, passion or urgency; blue conveys trust, calm or coldness; green suggests nature, health or wealth depending on context. Typography codes communicate through font choice: a serif font feels traditional and authoritative; a sans-serif font feels modern and clean; a handwritten font feels personal and informal.

Key Fact

The main media code categories are: camera (shot size, angle, movement); layout (hierarchy, rule of thirds, white space); colour (associations and connotations); typography (font style and weight); language (formal/informal register, tone, vocabulary); and imagery (choice of subject, composition, style).

Genre Conventions and Audience Expectations

A genre is a category of media product defined by recurring characteristics that audiences recognise and expect. Horror films use low-key lighting, discordant music and isolated settings because these are the genre's conventions. A thriller poster uses dark colours, large bold type and a single central figure in silhouette. A children's magazine uses bright primary colours, rounded fonts and cheerful photographs. These are all conventions: the accepted approaches that define how a genre looks, sounds and feels. When a creator works within genre conventions, they give audiences what they expect; when they subvert conventions deliberately, they create surprise or discomfort for artistic effect.

Genre conventions matter because audiences use them to make decisions: if a film poster uses the codes of the horror genre, a viewer who enjoys horror knows to watch it; a viewer who dislikes horror knows to avoid it. Conventions act as a contract between creator and audience. For a media professional, following conventions reduces risk — the product is immediately legible to the right audience. Innovation within conventions (e.g. a comedy that subverts horror tropes) is a recognised creative strategy, but innovation that ignores conventions entirely can alienate an audience that expected something familiar. Understanding conventions is a prerequisite for knowing when and how to break them.

Style, Mood and Tone

Beyond genre, every media product uses style, mood and tone to create an emotional response in the audience. Style is the overall visual and creative approach — minimalist, maximalist, retro, futuristic, hand-crafted. Mood is the emotional atmosphere the product creates — tense, joyful, nostalgic, energetic. Tone is the attitude of the communication — formal or informal, serious or playful, authoritative or conversational. These three elements work together through the careful combination of media codes: a product can feel tense through the combined use of dark colours, fast-cut editing, minor-key music and tight close-up shots, even without a single line of dialogue.

Applying Codes to Appeal to an Audience

The purpose of using media codes deliberately is to appeal to the target audience. A social media advert targeting young adults interested in sustainable fashion might use earthy, muted colour tones (colour code), hand-drawn typography (typography code), candid-style photography (imagery code) and informal language (language code) — all chosen because this audience associates those codes with authenticity and environmental values. Every code choice is, in effect, an audience choice: a decision about what this specific group of people will respond to positively.

Key Fact

Style, mood and tone work together to create audience response. Style = overall visual approach; mood = emotional atmosphere; tone = attitude of the communication. All three are constructed through deliberate use of media codes and must be matched to the target audience and genre conventions of the product.

Students frequently list codes correctly but stop at the description: "the poster uses red and black colours" gains minimal marks. The examiner needs you to explain the effect: "the poster uses red to signify danger and urgency, and black to create a sense of threat, which positions the audience to feel anxious before they have read a word of the copy." Always complete the chain: identify the code, describe how it is used, and explain what effect it is intended to have on the target audience. This applies whether you are analysing an existing product or justifying a creative decision in your own practical work.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing media codes in an exam, always work in three steps: identify the code, describe how it is used in this specific product, and explain the intended effect on the target audience. A response that does all three will reach Mastering level. Avoid general statements like "the colour makes it look professional" — instead be specific: "the use of navy blue and white, combined with a serif typeface, constructs connotations of authority and trustworthiness, which aligns with the target audience's expectations of a financial services brand."
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Media codes — including camera, layout, colour, typography, language and imagery — are the systems through which media products communicate meaning; every code choice should be deliberate and justifiable.
  • Genre conventions are the established norms audiences expect within a category of media; working within or against conventions is a creative choice with real audience impact.
  • Style, mood and tone are constructed through the combination of multiple codes; exam answers must link code choices to specific audience effects, not just describe what can be seen.

lessons.title: Legal, Ethical & Regulatory Considerations
lessons.description: Know the legal, ethical and regulatory rules every media creator must follow before publishing.
lessons.content_html:
Why Law and Ethics Matter in Media

Creating a media product does not happen in a vacuum. Every piece of content — a photograph, a music track, a piece of writing, a video clip — may be protected by law, subject to industry regulation or carry ethical responsibilities to the audience it reaches. Professional media creators must understand these obligations before they begin production, not after. Failing to do so can result in legal action, financial penalties, reputational damage or harm to the people depicted in the product.

Copyright and Intellectual Property

Copyright is the most important legal concept for media creators. It exists automatically when an original work is created — a photograph, a piece of music, a written article or a film — and gives the creator (or whoever owns the copyright) the exclusive right to control how that work is used. Using someone else's copyrighted material without permission is an infringement and can lead to legal action. Intellectual property is the broader category that includes copyright, trademarks (protecting brand names and logos) and patents (protecting inventions). Media creators must be able to demonstrate that every asset in their product is either their own original work, properly licensed, or covered by an appropriate usage right.

Key Fact

Copyright protects original creative works automatically from the moment of creation. In the UK, copyright in a photograph, film or written work typically lasts for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years. After this period, the work enters the public domain and can be used freely.

Licensed, Royalty-Free and Creative Commons Assets

When a media creator needs to use an asset they did not create — a stock photograph, a music track, a font — they have several legal options. A licensed asset requires the creator to seek formal permission from the copyright holder, often paying a fee. Royalty-free assets can be purchased for a one-off payment and then used without paying ongoing royalties every time the product is published or broadcast. Creative Commons (CC) licences are a standardised set of permissions granted by the copyright holder. A CC BY licence allows use as long as the creator is attributed; CC BY-NC adds the restriction that the work cannot be used for commercial purposes; CC BY-ND prohibits creating adapted versions. Public domain works have no copyright restrictions — either the copyright has expired or the creator has waived all rights. Choosing the right type of asset is a legal obligation, not merely a best practice.

If a media product features identifiable people — whether in photographs, video footage or named in text — the creator must obtain the appropriate permissions. A model release is a signed agreement from a person confirming that their image can be used in a specific way (e.g. in an advert). A location release grants permission to film or photograph on private property. Without these, the creator could face claims under privacy law or data protection legislation. In the UK, the Data Protection Act 2018 and the UK GDPR govern how personal data — including photographs that identify individuals — can be collected and used. Media creators working with children must also ensure parental consent is obtained before recording or publishing any content featuring under-18s.

Regulation and Age Ratings

The media industry is regulated by both government bodies and independent organisations to ensure content is appropriate for its intended audience. PEGI (Pan European Game Information) provides age ratings for video games: PEGI 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. These ratings are based on content analysis covering violence, language, sexual content, gambling and drug use, and are legally enforceable in the UK for the 12, 16 and 18 categories — retailers must not sell age-restricted games to younger buyers. The BBFC (British Board of Film Classification) classifies films for cinema and home release with ratings including U (suitable for all), PG (parental guidance), 12A/12, 15 and 18. (12A is the cinema certificate — under-12s may watch with an adult — while 12 is the equivalent for home video/DVD, where no one under 12 is admitted.) Like PEGI 12+ ratings, BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 certificates carry legal force for cinema admissions.

Key Fact

PEGI rates video games with five age categories: 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. The BBFC classifies films with: U, PG, 12A/12, 15 and 18. PEGI 12, 16 and 18 ratings are legally enforceable in UK retail; BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 certificates are legally enforced for cinema admission.

Students frequently mix up PEGI and BBFC, or claim that all ratings are "just a recommendation". PEGI rates games (not films); the BBFC rates films (and video works). Both systems have legally enforceable elements: PEGI 12, 16 and 18 are enforceable at UK retail points of sale; BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 certificates are enforced at UK cinemas. PEGI 3 and 7, and BBFC U and PG, are advisory rather than legally enforced. In an exam, state which body rates which type of product, name the specific rating categories, and distinguish between advisory and legally enforced ratings — this level of precision is what takes an answer to Mastering.

Ethical Considerations in Media

Beyond legal obligations, media creators must consider the ethical impact of their work — particularly in how people are represented. Stereotyping is the use of oversimplified or inaccurate generalisations about groups of people. Repeated stereotyping in media can reinforce prejudice and cause real harm to the groups depicted. Ethical creators consider whether their content fairly represents people of different genders, ethnicities, ages, abilities and backgrounds. Related concerns include offensive content (material that demeans or dehumanises individuals or groups), privacy (filming or publishing images of people without consent), and the accuracy of information presented as factual. Ethical responsibilities extend to online content: using photoshopped imagery without disclosure, or creating misleading advertising, are both legal and ethical concerns even when technically permitted.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For legal and regulatory questions, precision is essential. Always name the correct body (PEGI for games, BBFC for films) and the specific rating categories — never write "the ratings board" generically. When discussing copyright, distinguish between the type of licence: "royalty-free" is not the same as "copyright-free" or "free to use". For ethics questions, name a specific concern (stereotyping, privacy, representation) and explain both what it is and why it matters to the audience or the individuals depicted, not just that "it could cause offence".
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Copyright protects original creative works automatically; media creators must ensure every asset is their own, properly licensed, Creative Commons-approved or in the public domain — using copyrighted material without permission is an infringement.
  • PEGI rates video games (3, 7, 12, 16, 18) and the BBFC rates films (U, PG, 12A/12, 15, 18); PEGI 12, 16 and 18 and BBFC 12A/12, 15 and 18 are legally enforced, while lower categories are advisory.
  • Ethical responsibilities include avoiding harmful stereotyping, respecting privacy, obtaining model and location releases, and ensuring content accurately represents the people and facts it depicts.

lessons.title: Pre-production Documents: Mood Boards, Mind Maps & Visualisation Diagrams
lessons.description: The purpose of pre-production planning and how mood boards, mind maps and visualisation diagrams are used.
lessons.content_html:
Why Plan Before You Create?

Before any media product is made, a creator must plan. Pre-production planning is the stage where ideas are explored, resources are identified and decisions are made about what the final product will look like. Skipping this stage is one of the most common reasons media projects run over time or miss the client's brief. Good pre-production documents act as a roadmap: they keep the creator on track, help communicate ideas to a client or team, and provide evidence that a brief has been understood.

Key Fact

The three main pre-production documents for planning the look and feel of a media product are mood boards, mind maps and visualisation diagrams. Each serves a different purpose: mood boards gather inspiration, mind maps generate and link ideas, and visualisation diagrams plan the layout of a specific product.

Mood Boards

A mood board is a collage of visual references that captures the intended style, colour palette and tone of a product. A designer might include photographs, magazine cuttings, colour swatches, font samples and texture examples. The mood board does not show the layout of the final product — it shows the feeling and aesthetic that the creator is aiming for. For example, a mood board for a charity campaign might use muted greens, handwritten-style fonts and photographs of outdoor spaces to communicate a natural, calm atmosphere.

Mood boards are particularly useful at the very start of a project. They help the creator explore whether an idea will work visually before any time is spent making assets, and they give the client a clear impression of the proposed direction. A client who approves a mood board has, in effect, approved the visual language of the product before a single file has been opened in an editing application. This reduces expensive re-working later in the production process.

A mood board typically contains: images sourced from the internet, magazines or photography; colour swatches showing the planned colour palette; font samples demonstrating the intended typography; texture references (e.g. rough paper, smooth metal); and brief annotations explaining why each element has been chosen. In digital form, a mood board might be assembled in software such as Canva, PowerPoint or Adobe Photoshop. There is no single fixed format — what matters is that the visual references clearly communicate the intended style to someone who has not yet seen any part of the finished product.

Mind Maps

A mind map is used during the idea-generation phase to explore all possible angles of a brief before committing to one direction. The central topic or brief is placed in the middle of the page, and branches radiate outward to show related ideas, sub-topics, themes and potential approaches. Further sub-branches can explore each idea in more detail. Mind maps are non-linear, which means a creator is not forced to think in a straight line — they can jump between ideas and notice unexpected connections.

For a media project, a mind map might branch from a central brief such as “design a poster for a local music festival” into branches covering target audience, possible colour schemes, image styles, text content, competitor examples and potential slogans. The mind map is typically hand-drawn or produced digitally using free tools such as Coggle or MindMeister. It is not a polished document intended for the client — it is a thinking tool used by the creator to ensure the brief has been fully explored before any decisions are locked in.

The key difference is purpose. A mood board is about visual style — it gathers images and colours to communicate how the product will look and feel. A mind map is about ideas — it maps out what the product could contain, how it could be structured and what approaches are possible. A mood board is often shown to a client; a mind map is usually a personal or team planning tool. In practice, a creator might produce a mind map first to generate ideas, then develop the most promising idea into a mood board to communicate the visual direction to a client or teacher.

Visualisation Diagrams

A visualisation diagram is a rough sketch of what the final product will look like. Unlike a mood board, which captures style, a visualisation diagram shows specific layout: where the heading will sit, how large the main image will be, where the body text will appear and what colours will be used in each area. It is produced for static or single-page products such as posters, flyers, magazine pages, DVD covers or single web pages. It is not suitable for moving-image products such as videos or animations — a storyboard is used for those instead.

Key Fact

A visualisation diagram should include: the overall dimensions and orientation of the product; placeholder boxes for images; approximate positions and sizes of all text elements (headings, body copy, slogans); the planned colour scheme; and annotations explaining design choices such as font style or why a particular image will be used. Every element should be labelled.

Visualisation diagrams are typically hand-drawn on A4 or A3 paper, though digital tools can be used. The level of detail should be enough that someone else could pick up the diagram and understand what the finished product is meant to look like. They do not need to be artistically perfect — clear annotation is more important than drawing skill. When submitting coursework for this unit, students must produce pre-production documents including visualisation diagrams as evidence of planning before they begin creating their final product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Exam questions often ask you to ‘explain the purpose’ of a specific pre-production document. Do not confuse mood boards, mind maps and visualisation diagrams. The mood board is about visual style and inspiration; the mind map is about generating and connecting ideas; the visualisation diagram shows the planned layout of a specific product. If a question says ‘suitable for a poster’, the answer is a visualisation diagram — not a storyboard. Storyboards are reserved for moving-image or animated products. Always link the document to both its purpose and the type of product it suits.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pre-production planning documents are produced before any media asset is created; they ensure the brief is understood, ideas are explored and the visual direction is agreed before production begins.
  • Mood boards gather visual inspiration (colour, style, texture, font); mind maps generate and connect ideas around a brief; visualisation diagrams sketch the specific layout and content of a static product.
  • Visualisation diagrams are used for static, single-page products such as posters and magazine pages; moving-image products require a storyboard instead.

lessons.title: Storyboards, Scripts & Work Plans
lessons.description: How storyboards, scripts and work plans are used to plan moving-image, audio and time-based media projects.
lessons.content_html:
Planning Moving-Image and Audio Products

When a media product involves movement, speech or sound unfolding over time — such as a video, animation or podcast — a visualisation diagram is not enough. Creators need documents that capture sequence, timing and sound. The three key planning documents for time-based products are storyboards, scripts and work plans. Together these documents ensure that a complex, multi-stage production stays focused on the original brief throughout the entire process.

Storyboards

A storyboard is a sequence of drawn frames, arranged like a comic strip, that maps out a moving-image or animated product shot by shot. Each frame represents a single shot or scene change, and the space around each frame is used for annotations. A typical storyboard frame includes: a sketch of what the camera will see; a note of the camera angle and shot type (e.g. close-up, wide shot, bird's-eye view); the duration of the shot in seconds; a description of any camera movement (pan, tilt, zoom); the transition to the next shot (cut, dissolve, fade); and notes on the audio — dialogue, voiceover, music or sound effects.

Key Fact

A storyboard frame should include: a sketch of the scene; the shot type and camera angle; the duration of the shot; any camera movement; the transition to the next shot; and audio notes including dialogue, music and sound effects. All six elements should be present for a complete storyboard.

Storyboards are used for videos, animations, advertisements and any other moving-image product. They allow the creator to spot problems — such as a sequence of shots that will be confusing for the viewer, or a scene that requires props or locations that are unavailable — before any filming or animation begins. A well-drawn storyboard also helps when working with a team, because each person can see exactly what is needed for every shot without relying on spoken instructions.

Shot types describe the distance between the camera and the subject: an extreme close-up fills the frame with a single feature (such as an eye); a close-up shows the face; a medium shot shows the upper body; a wide shot shows the full subject in their environment; and an extreme wide shot establishes a location. Camera angles describe the vertical position of the camera: a low angle looks up at the subject and makes them appear powerful; a high angle looks down and makes them appear small or vulnerable; a bird's-eye view is directly overhead; and a worm's-eye view is directly below, looking up. Knowing these terms allows a creator to annotate storyboard frames precisely and communicate their intentions clearly to a filming team or animator.

Scripts

A script is the written plan for the words and sounds in an audio or video production. A video script typically shows dialogue or voiceover on one side of the page alongside a brief description of the matching visuals, so that audio and visual elements can be produced in sync. A radio or podcast script focuses entirely on the spoken content and sound effects, including instructions such as “fade in music” or “pause for two seconds”. Scripts are essential for any production involving speech because they ensure the content is accurate, on-message and the right length before recording begins. A client reviewing a script can check the tone and message without needing to watch a rough cut.

A production script for a video typically includes: the speaker's name before each line of dialogue; descriptions of any narration or voiceover; sound effect and music cues (e.g. “SFX: door slam” or “Music: upbeat track fades in”); scene headings indicating location and time of day; and stage directions describing what is happening on screen. A radio or podcast script follows a similar structure but replaces visual descriptions with timing notes. The script should be formatted clearly so that any performer or technician can follow it without needing to ask questions.

Work Plans and Production Schedules

A work plan (also called a production schedule) is a time-management document. It breaks the entire project down into individual tasks, assigns a deadline and a responsible person to each task, and lists the resources required for each stage. A work plan for a video project might include tasks such as: write script (Day 1-2); film location footage (Day 3-4); record voiceover (Day 5); edit footage (Day 6-8); export and review (Day 9); submit (Day 10). Milestones — key points by which a significant stage must be complete — are often highlighted separately within the plan.

Key Fact

A work plan should always include contingency time: a buffer period built into the schedule to allow for unexpected problems such as equipment failure, illness or a scene that needs to be reshot. Without contingency, any delay will cause the final deadline to be missed. Good planning anticipates problems rather than ignoring them.

Work plans are particularly important when working to a client deadline, as they make it possible to see at a glance whether the project is on track. They also help when resources must be shared — for example, if a camera is only available for two days, the work plan ensures that filming is scheduled within that window. A realistic work plan considers not only how long each task will take in ideal conditions, but also includes time for review, client feedback and final corrections before submission.
lessons.exam_tip_html: If an exam question asks you to describe a storyboard, always include detail about what is annotated on each frame — shot type, camera angle, duration, transition and audio notes. Saying ‘it shows what each scene looks like’ alone will score only 1 mark. For work plan questions, remember that contingency is a required element: a plan without built-in buffer time is incomplete. If the question gives a scenario with a tight deadline, always mention contingency as part of your answer, even for lower-mark questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Storyboards plan moving-image and animated products shot by shot, with each frame annotated with shot type, camera angle, duration, transitions, camera movement and audio notes.
  • Scripts set out the spoken words, sound effects and music cues for audio and video productions, ensuring content is accurate and the right length before any recording takes place.
  • Work plans break a project into tasks with deadlines, milestones and responsible persons, and must always include contingency time to protect the final deadline against unexpected delays.

lessons.title: Planning Assets, Hardware, Software & File Management
lessons.description: Identifying assets needed for a media product, the hardware and software used, file formats and good file management.
lessons.content_html:
Identifying the Assets You Need

Before any media product can be created, a producer must identify every asset that will be needed. Assets fall into several categories: images (photographs, illustrations, icons); audio (background music, sound effects, voiceover recordings); video clips (footage, screen recordings); graphics (logos, charts, diagrams); and text (copy, captions, headings). Listing all required assets at the planning stage prevents the common problem of reaching the editing phase and discovering that a critical file is missing, unavailable or in the wrong format.

For each asset, a creator should note: what the asset is; whether it will be created from scratch, sourced from a stock library, or provided by the client; who is responsible for obtaining or creating it; and any legal considerations such as copyright or licence requirements. This asset list becomes part of the pre-production documentation and helps ensure the project remains on schedule.

Hardware and Software for Asset Creation

Different asset types require different hardware and software. A digital camera or smartphone is used to capture photographs; a microphone and audio interface capture high-quality audio; a graphics tablet allows artists to draw digitally; a scanner converts physical drawings into digital files; and a powerful computer is needed for video rendering. Choosing the right hardware for the job affects the quality and speed of asset creation.

Software choices are equally important. Common applications include: Adobe Photoshop or GIMP for editing still images; Adobe Illustrator or Inkscape for creating vector graphics; Adobe Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve for video editing; Audacity or Adobe Audition for audio editing; and Canva or Adobe InDesign for layout and publication design. Each application is specialised for a particular type of asset; using the wrong tool can lead to poor-quality outputs or unnecessary file conversions.

Key Fact

For the exam, you need to know the correct hardware and software pairing for common asset types: still images (camera/scanner + Photoshop/GIMP); audio (microphone + Audacity/Audition); vector graphics (graphics tablet + Illustrator/Inkscape); video (video camera + Premiere Pro/DaVinci Resolve); publication layout (computer + InDesign/Canva).

Understanding file formats is essential for saving and sharing assets correctly. For images: JPEG (lossy compression, small file size, best for photographs on the web); PNG (lossless, supports transparency, best for logos and graphics with sharp edges); GIF (lossless, supports simple animation, limited to 256 colours, best for short looping web animations); TIFF (lossless, very large files, used in print production where maximum quality is needed). For audio: MP3 (lossy compression, small file size, good for web streaming and podcasts); WAV (uncompressed, very large files, used in professional audio production where editing quality matters). For video: MP4 using the H.264 codec (efficient lossy compression, widely compatible, standard for web and social media delivery). For print-ready documents and layouts: PDF (preserves formatting across all devices and print setups). Choosing the correct format depends on the intended use: web delivery favours small, compressed files; professional editing and print favour uncompressed or lossless formats.

File Naming and Version Control

Good file naming and version control practices are essential in any media project. File names should be descriptive, consistent and free from spaces or special characters that can cause compatibility problems across different operating systems. A sensible naming convention might be: project-name_asset-type_version-number, for example charity-poster_hero-image_v3.psd. Version numbers allow a creator to keep earlier iterations of a file in case a later version needs to be rolled back. Without version control, overwriting a working file with a broken revision can cause hours of lost work.

Key Fact

A sensible folder structure for a media project separates assets by type. A top-level project folder might contain sub-folders named: images, audio, video, graphics, exports and working-files. Keeping all assets for one project in a single, well-organised folder structure ensures files are easy to find, easy to share with a team and easy to hand over to a client at the end of the project.

In a professional context, poor file naming has real consequences. A file named “final2_ACTUAL_v3_USE THIS ONE.jpg” is a common but damaging mistake: if a colleague is asked to use the correct version, they cannot identify it at a glance. Spaces in file names can break web links and script references. Special characters such as & or # can cause errors in some operating systems and web servers. In team projects, file naming conventions should be agreed at the start of the project and documented in the work plan so that everyone applies them consistently. In a school context, clear file names also make it far easier for an assessor to navigate submitted work.
lessons.exam_tip_html: File format questions are common and have specific correct answers. Learn the four image formats (JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF) and be able to state whether each is lossy or lossless and give one typical use case. The most common mistake is saying PNG is suitable for photographs on the web — JPEG is better for photographs because PNG produces a larger file. PNG is better for logos and graphics with transparency. GIF is for simple web animations. TIFF is for print. If the question asks you to justify your choice, always mention both the purpose (what it will be used for) and a relevant property (file size, quality, transparency support).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Assets for a media product include images, audio, video, graphics and text; each type requires specific hardware (e.g. camera, microphone) and software (e.g. Photoshop, Audacity) to create or edit.
  • File format choice depends on the intended use: JPEG for web photographs; PNG for graphics with transparency; GIF for simple animations; TIFF for print; MP3 for web audio; WAV for professional editing; MP4 for video delivery; PDF for print-ready layouts.
  • Good file management — descriptive naming, version numbering and logical folder structures — prevents lost work, speeds up teamwork and makes it easier for clients and assessors to navigate submitted files.

lessons.title: Properties of Media & Preparing Products for Distribution
lessons.description: How image resolution, colour depth, compression and bitrate affect quality and file size when optimising media products.
lessons.content_html:
Why Properties Matter

Every media file has technical properties that determine its visual or audio quality and its file size. Understanding these properties is essential because file size and quality always exist in tension: higher quality means larger files, and larger files take longer to download, stream or load. A media creator must balance these properties for the specific platform and audience. A print-quality photograph that is perfect in a magazine will be far too large for a web page, where a viewer expects the page to load in under two seconds. Preparing a product for distribution means making deliberate decisions about each technical property to optimise the file for its purpose.

Image Resolution and Dimensions

Resolution describes how much detail an image contains. For print, resolution is measured in dots per inch (DPI): professional print output requires at least 300 DPI, and images printed at lower resolutions appear blurry or pixelated. For screen display (websites, presentations, social media), 72 to 96 pixels per inch (PPI) is sufficient because monitors display fewer pixels per physical inch than a printer lays down ink dots. Sending a 300 DPI image to a website is wasteful — it produces an unnecessarily large file with no visible quality benefit to the viewer.

Dimensions are measured in pixels (width x height). A full-width website banner might need to be 1920 x 1080 pixels, while a social media profile picture might only need to be 400 x 400 pixels. Resizing an image to the exact dimensions required for the platform reduces file size without the need for aggressive compression. As a rule, always reduce image dimensions before uploading to a web platform, rather than relying on the platform to resize the image for you.

Key Fact

Print images require at least 300 DPI (dots per inch) to appear sharp. Screen images require only 72 to 96 PPI (pixels per inch) because monitor displays do not resolve detail as finely as printed ink. Using a 300 DPI image on a website wastes bandwidth without improving the viewer's experience.

Bit Depth and Colour

Bit depth determines how many colours an image can contain. A 1-bit image contains only black and white (2 colours). An 8-bit image can contain 256 colours — enough for simple graphics and GIF animations, but not for photographs. A 24-bit image uses 8 bits per channel across three channels (red, green, blue), giving over 16 million possible colours — this is referred to as true colour and is the standard for photographs and complex digital artwork. A 32-bit image adds an alpha channel for transparency information on top of the 24-bit colour data. Higher bit depth produces better colour accuracy but increases file size.

GIF files are limited to an 8-bit palette of 256 colours. This is why GIFs look flat or banded when used for photographs — the limited palette cannot accurately represent the millions of subtle tones in a photo. GIF is best reserved for simple graphics, text-based animations and logos where only a few colours are needed. PNG supports both 8-bit (PNG-8) and 24-bit (PNG-24) colour. PNG-8 produces smaller files than PNG-24 but with the same 256-colour limit as GIF; PNG-24 supports full true colour and is appropriate for photographs needing transparency. Choosing between PNG-8 and PNG-24 is itself a file size vs quality decision that a creator must make based on the complexity of the image.

Compression: Lossy vs Lossless

Compression is the process of reducing a file's size so it can be stored, transferred or streamed more efficiently. Lossy compression permanently removes data that the human eye or ear is least likely to notice, producing a significantly smaller file at the cost of some quality. JPEG and MP3 are lossy formats. Lossless compression encodes the data more efficiently without discarding anything, so the original can be perfectly reconstructed. PNG, GIF and WAV are lossless. The choice between lossy and lossless depends on the purpose: professional editing and print require lossless quality; web delivery and streaming benefit from the smaller file sizes that lossy compression provides.

Each time a JPEG image is opened, edited and re-saved, another round of lossy compression is applied. The quality loss accumulates with every save, a phenomenon sometimes called generation loss. After several cycles, visible artefacts appear: blocky patterns around edges, smearing in areas of fine detail, and washed-out colours. This is why professional photographers and designers always keep the original high-resolution RAW or TIFF file and export a JPEG only at the very end of the editing process — never editing from the JPEG directly. The same principle applies to audio: always keep the original WAV or uncompressed source file and export the MP3 as the final delivery format.

Bitrate for Audio and Video

Bitrate is the amount of data used per second of audio or video playback, measured in kilobits per second (kbps) or megabits per second (Mbps). For audio, a bitrate of 128 kbps is considered acceptable for casual listening; 320 kbps is considered high quality for MP3. For video, a bitrate of 5 to 8 Mbps is typical for 1080p HD streaming; 4K video may require 35 to 45 Mbps or more. Higher bitrate produces better quality but larger files that require more bandwidth to stream. A video intended for social media upload will be exported at a lower bitrate than the same video destined for a cinema screen or broadcast.

Key Fact

Bitrate directly controls the trade-off between quality and file size for audio and video. Standard MP3 bitrates range from 128 kbps (acceptable quality) to 320 kbps (high quality). Standard video bitrates for web delivery range from 1 Mbps (low quality, small file) to 8 Mbps or more for 1080p HD. Higher bitrate files require faster internet connections to stream without buffering.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about properties often ask you to ‘justify’ a choice — which means you must explain why a particular value or format was chosen, not just name it. For DPI, always link the number to the output: 300 DPI because it is going to print; 72 PPI because it is for the web. For compression, always state whether it is lossy or lossless and why that matters for the purpose. For bitrate, always mention the quality-versus-file-size trade-off. These justification chains are what separate Secure from Mastering answers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Print images require at least 300 DPI; screen images require 72 to 96 PPI; using a higher resolution than needed wastes file size without improving quality for the viewer.
  • Bit depth determines how many colours an image can contain: 8-bit supports 256 colours; 24-bit supports over 16 million (true colour). Higher bit depth increases file size.
  • Lossy compression (JPEG, MP3) permanently removes data to reduce file size; lossless compression (PNG, WAV) reduces size without losing data. Bitrate controls the data-per-second in audio and video, directly trading quality for file size.

lessons.title: Distribution Platforms & Considerations
lessons.description: The platforms used to distribute media products and the key factors to consider when choosing how to reach an audience.
lessons.content_html:
How Media Products Reach Audiences

Once a media product has been created, it must be distributed — shared with the intended audience through an appropriate channel. A distribution platform is the channel through which a product reaches its viewers, listeners or readers. Choosing the right platform requires understanding the target audience, the type of product, the file formats supported, and practical considerations such as cost, accessibility and the technical requirements of each channel. A poor distribution choice can mean a well-made product never reaches the people it was created for.

Web and Streaming Platforms

Web-based distribution means hosting a product on a website or video-streaming platform so that users can access it via a browser or dedicated app. Video platforms such as YouTube and Vimeo allow creators to upload video content that can be viewed by anyone with an internet connection, using adaptive streaming to deliver the right quality for the viewer's connection speed. Audio can be distributed via podcast platforms such as Spotify, Apple Podcasts or Anchor. Web-based distribution is typically free or low-cost, allows instant worldwide reach, and makes it easy to update or remove content. However, it requires the audience to have a reliable internet connection, and content can be easily copied or downloaded without permission.

Key Fact

Web and streaming platforms (websites, YouTube, Spotify, podcast apps) offer instant worldwide reach, easy updating and low cost, but require the audience to have an internet connection. File formats must match what the platform accepts: most video platforms require MP4; most podcast platforms require MP3; most websites display JPEG and PNG images.

Social Media Platforms

Social media platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and X (formerly Twitter) are widely used to distribute still images, short videos, and audio content directly to followers and their wider networks. Social media distribution benefits from built-in sharing mechanics — a post can be shared, liked and commented on, dramatically extending the reach of a product beyond the creator's own following at no additional cost. However, each platform has its own specifications: Instagram favours square or portrait images (1080 x 1080 px or 1080 x 1350 px); TikTok uses portrait video at 9:16 aspect ratio; and all platforms apply their own compression on upload, reducing quality. A media creator must therefore export assets at the correct dimensions and in the accepted format for each platform before uploading.

App stores such as the Apple App Store and Google Play Store allow creators to distribute interactive media products — games, interactive presentations, educational apps — directly to smartphone and tablet users. App store distribution provides a large, built-in audience and a trusted payment system, but requires the product to pass a review process (which can take days or weeks) and the creator must pay a developer registration fee. The app must also be built to meet the technical requirements of each platform (iOS or Android), which often means producing two separate versions. App stores are most appropriate for interactive, software-based products rather than passive media such as videos or podcasts.

Physical Media and Print

Physical media includes DVDs, Blu-rays, USB drives, printed posters, magazines and books. Physical distribution is appropriate when the target audience has limited or no internet access, when a high-quality print product is required (such as a photographic exhibition or a professional brochure), or when a product needs to be provided in a format that can be used without any internet connection. Physical distribution is more expensive than digital — manufacturing, packaging, and postage all add cost — and updates or corrections cannot be made once a product has been printed or pressed. However, physical products have a tangible presence that many audiences value, and they are not subject to platform changes or removal.

Broadcast Distribution

Broadcast distribution involves transmitting video or audio content via television or radio to a mass audience simultaneously. Traditional broadcast (terrestrial television, satellite, cable, and FM/DAB radio) reaches very large audiences, including those without internet access, but requires formal agreements with broadcasters and is expensive and difficult to access for independent creators. Increasingly, broadcast-style content is also distributed via internet-connected television platforms such as BBC iPlayer, ITVX and Channel 4 streaming services, which combine the wide reach of broadcast with the on-demand flexibility of web streaming. For the vast majority of student and small-scale media projects, broadcast is not a realistic distribution method.

Accessibility means ensuring that a product can be used by people with a range of abilities and access needs. For digital distribution, this includes: providing subtitles or closed captions for videos (essential for d/Deaf viewers and useful in noisy environments); using alt text for images on websites (so screen readers can describe them to visually impaired users); ensuring colour contrast meets minimum standards (important for colour-blind users); and providing transcripts for audio-only content such as podcasts. For physical distribution, accessibility considerations include large-print versions of documents and Braille alternatives. When choosing a distribution platform, a creator should consider whether the platform supports these accessibility features or whether they must be added manually.

Key Fact

When choosing a distribution platform, four key considerations are: the target audience (demographics, internet access, device ownership); the file formats the platform accepts; the cost to the creator and to the audience; and accessibility (whether the platform supports subtitles, alt text, screen readers and other assistive features). No single platform is ideal for every product and every audience.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Distribution questions often ask you to ‘justify’ or ‘evaluate’ a platform choice. Avoid simply listing platforms — the marks come from linking each platform to the specific audience and product in the scenario. For example: ‘YouTube is appropriate because the target audience is 13-to-25-year-olds who regularly use the platform on smartphones, and MP4 is the accepted format.’ Always consider at least one disadvantage or limitation, as a balanced response scores higher than a one-sided answer. If the question mentions a specific audience group (e.g. older adults, people without internet access), physical media or broadcast should be discussed as alternatives.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Distribution platforms include web and streaming (YouTube, Spotify), social media (Instagram, TikTok), app stores, physical media (DVD, print) and broadcast (TV, radio); each suits different products, audiences and budgets.
  • Choosing the right platform requires matching the audience's demographics and internet access, the file formats the platform accepts, the cost to the creator and user, and the accessibility features available.
  • Accessibility considerations such as subtitles for video, alt text for images and transcripts for audio must be built into distribution plans, not added as an afterthought.

practice_questions.text:
A student has created a 3-minute promotional video for a local charity. The charity wants to reach as wide an audience as possible, including older adults who may not use social media.

Discuss which distribution platforms would be most appropriate for the charity's promotional video.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying at least two platforms and evaluating each in relation to the scenario. YouTube or a website: large reach, free, accessible on smart TVs as well as computers and phones, accepted format is MP4, supports captions — suitable for the general public including older adults who do use the internet. Social media (Facebook specifically): older adults are actually one of the largest Facebook demographics, so this may reach more of the target group than TikTok would; shares can extend reach virally. practice_questions.text:
A games developer has created an interactive educational quiz for secondary school students. They are deciding whether to distribute the quiz via a website, a dedicated app on the Apple App Store, or on physical USB drives sent to schools.

Evaluate the suitability of each distribution method for this product and audience, and recommend which option the developer should choose.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation of all three options. Website: low cost, instant updates possible, no download required, works on any device with a browser — but relies on school internet connectivity, which may be unreliable; no revenue model without a subscription. App store: large built-in audience, trusted payment system, works offline once downloaded — but requires a developer fee, review process, and two separate builds for iOS and Android; schools may restrict app installation on managed devices. USB drives: works without internet, can be used on any computer — but expensive to produce, cannot be updated once distributed, risk of data being copied or the drive being lost; no analytics on usage. A clear, substantiated recommendation is reached (website is likely the strongest choice for a school audience given device variety and the ability to update content), with counter-arguments acknowledged. Secure (5-6 marks): All three options addressed with some application and an attempt at a recommendation. Developing (3-4 marks): Two options addressed, limited application. Emerging (1-2 marks): One option or basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]
